statement: In healthy young adults, mostly university students, who drank beer in a laboratory to the same level of intoxication and then had a supervised night in bed, beer with added caffeine compared with the same beer without caffeine did not detectably change next-morning hangover severity (Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 against 1.45, d = 0.13) or the share with any hangover (61% against 69%), nor self-reported time to fall asleep, time asleep or morning sleepiness, in a randomized comparison of 28 and 36 people; the caffeine group rated its sleep quality better (d = 0.64), mainly because of morning alertness items (Rohsenow et al., 2014). Evidence is insufficient to say whether caffeine changes hangover: the intervals include a moderate difference either way (editors' calculation: any hangover from 32 percentage points lower to 15 higher with caffeine), sleep was self-reported, energy drinks and other amounts were not tested, and the study is a later analysis of a trial designed for driving outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, beer with added caffeine did not change the next-morning hangover compared with the same beer without caffeine, and people did not report sleeping less. The study was small, so a moderate effect either way cannot be ruled out, and energy drinks were not tested.
population: 64 healthy adults aged 21 to 30 (89% university students) without drinking problems, in a laboratory study in Boston
exposure: Beer with added caffeine, at the concentration of a commercial caffeinated beer, drunk to a set level of intoxication (amounts are on the study card)
comparator: A randomized group drinking the same beer without caffeine to the same level
outcome: Next-morning Acute Hangover Scale (severity and any hangover); self-reported sleep quality, time to fall asleep and time asleep; Stanford Sleepiness Scale
magnitude: Caffeinated against non-caffeinated beer: Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 (SD 0.84) against 1.45 (0.89), d = 0.13 (editors' 95% CI for d −0.63 to 0.38); any hangover 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19 (editors' risk difference −8.7 percentage points, 95% CI −32 to 15); sleep quality 4.45 against 4.16, d = 0.64 (95% CI of the difference 0.057 to 0.517), better with caffeine; time to fall asleep d = 0.28, time asleep d = 0.21, sleepiness d = 0.23, none significant.

evidence.locator: Table 2, Acute Hangover Scale score and Hangover incidence rows; Results › Hangover, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Hangover severity 1.34 (SD 0.84) with caffeine against 1.45 (0.89) without, d = 0.13; any hangover 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19; neither significant (n = 28 and 36).

evidence.extracted: Self-reported minutes to fall asleep (36.5 with caffeine against 23.2 without), minutes asleep (390.7 against 404.7) and Stanford Sleepiness (2.52 against 2.78) did not differ significantly (d = 0.28, 0.21, 0.23).

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness
evidence.locator: Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: The caffeine group rated average sleep quality better than the group given beer without caffeine (4.45, SD 0.41, against 4.16, SD 0.49; t(62) = 2.49; d = 0.64); split afterwards, the difference lay more in morning alertness and concentration items (d = 0.42, p < 0.10) than in night-time items (d = 0.30).

evidence.page: PMC HTML, 1. Introduction; Results › 2.4 Participant characteristics; 3. Discussion
evidence.locator: 1. Introduction, 4th paragraph; 2.1 Overview of study; Results › 2.4 Participant characteristics, 1st paragraph; 3. Discussion, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: A secondary analysis of a randomized trial designed to study driving, comparing its two alcohol groups (completers only, 28 and 36); the authors acknowledge low power and that results may differ with other amounts of alcohol or caffeine and with older people.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomization, blinding to caffeine and attrition are not reported in this paper; a later secondary analysis with self-reported outcomes and a sleep-quality score split after the fact.

indirectness.note: Caffeine added to beer at one concentration, in young adults with a full night in bed; energy drinks, other amounts and the short sleep of real nights out were not tested.

imprecision.note: 64 people; the interval for any hangover runs from 32 percentage points lower to 15 higher (editors' calculation).

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. Insufficient evidence rather than no detectable change, because the intervals include moderate effects either way. The authors' statement that people who believe caffeine affects hangover are misinformed goes beyond these data. Single study.
